name: King’s Gambit
summary: The King’s Gambit (2.f4) sacrifices a pawn for rapid development and a direct assault, the boldest of the romantic openings.
intro: The King’s Gambit, 1.e4 e5 2.f4, is the emblem of romantic chess: White offers the f-pawn to rip open lines and hunt the black king. After 2...exf4 the accepted lines lead to some of the most spectacular attacking games ever played.

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The King's Gambit arises after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4, when White sacrifices a pawn to deflect Black's e5-pawn and seize the centre with a later d4 and rapid development. In return for the pawn, White gains the open f-file, a strong pawn on e4, and quick attacking chances against Black's king. It is the emblem of romantic nineteenth-century chess, prizing initiative and open lines over material.

White's plan is to recapture the f4-pawn or use the open f-file, castle kingside quickly, and throw the pieces at Black's position before Black consolidates the extra pawn. Black, in turn, aims either to return the pawn for smooth development or to cling to it and weather the storm. The struggle between White's attacking energy and Black's material and structural soundness gives the opening its enduring drama.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The classical continuation is 3.Nf3, the King's Knight Gambit, preventing the checking ...Qh4+ and preparing to develop and castle. Black's traditional reply 3...g5 tries to hold the extra pawn by building a defensive chain, though it can loosen the kingside; more modern treatments favour returning the pawn with lines such as 3...d5 for free development. Another well-known branch is 3.Bc4, the Bishop's Gambit, which allows ...Qh4+ but gains time by developing toward f7.

Beyond these, White sometimes plays quieter or gambit-declining setups, but the sharpest battles come when Black grabs and defends the f4-pawn. In every case the recurring themes are the open f-file, pressure on f7, and the fight for the e5- and d4-squares. Precise defence is essential for Black, since a single slip can hand White a devastating attack.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The King's Gambit was among the most popular and celebrated openings of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the era of romantic, sacrifice-laden chess, and it features in many of the classic brilliancies of that age. As defensive technique improved, it became less common at the top level because Black gained reliable methods of neutralising the attack and keeping the extra pawn. It nevertheless remains a beloved surprise weapon, admired for the rich, imbalanced positions and attacking chances it produces.
